answer:
1. The animation shows how much inflation can erode a retiree's income. It uses US consumer prices (CPI-U) and asks how often a fixed annual raise level, such as 2%, 3%, 3.1% or 6.38%, has kept up with the price rises seen in past stretches of time. It is labeled "US only · history, not a forecast."

2. Bars are added one at a time, each for a higher yearly raise level. They run from 2% to 3%, then 3.1%, then 6.38%. Each bar grows longer, and its label shows the share of historical stretches that raise level covered. Those shares are 2.4% for a 2% raise, 42.4% for 3%, "half" for 3.1%, and "all" for 6.38%. The 6.38% bar is tagged "Carl's stretch." In the last two frames a yellow "ILLUSTRATIVE" tag appears. Frame 4 adds the note "a median of the past, not an expectation."

3. A small yearly raise has rarely been enough to keep up with prices in the past. A 2% raise covered only about 2.4% of historical stretches. A 3% raise covered about 42%. About 3.1% covered half. Covering every stretch would have taken about 6.38% a year, which was the worst stretch, "Carl's." So an income that stays flat, or rises only slightly, would have lost buying power in many historical periods. The labels say this is history and not a forecast.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that a payout that never rises, or rises only a little each year, may lose purchasing power. They might then want to look at the inflation protection offered by the two annuity options. The animation does not say that.

5. That takeaway is my own conclusion, not something the animation states. The animation only shows the historical comparison and warns that it is not a forecast or an expectation.
